concept.name: Long straddle
concept.definition: A long straddle is the simultaneous purchase of a call and a put on the same underlying, at the same strike price (typically at-the-money) and the same expiration date. The position profits if the underlying moves far enough in either direction to overcome the combined premium paid.
concept.intuition: You are buying a big move without picking a direction: if the stock swings hard either way one leg pays off, and if it goes nowhere both legs decay.
concept.mechanics: Cost = call premium + put premium; breakevens at expiration are K +/- total premium. The position is long volatility and long gamma, with maximum loss limited to the premium paid if the underlying pins the strike at expiration.
concept.formula: Payoff at expiration = |S_T - K| - (C + P), per share, where C and P are the call and put premiums; breakevens = K + (C + P) and K - (C + P).
concept.failure_modes: The market prices straddles to the expected move, so the buyer loses if realized volatility undershoots implied volatility — the classic post-earnings 'IV crush' loss even when the stock moves. Time decay is steepest for ATM straddles near expiration.
concept.misconceptions: A straddle does not profit from any move, only from moves larger than the premium implies; buying a straddle before a known event means paying an event-inflated premium that typically collapses when the news is out.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, buy the $100 call for $3.00 and the $100 put for $2.50 (total $5.50). XYZ must finish above $105.50 or below $94.50 at expiration to profit; a finish at $100 loses the full $550.
